question.problem:
Consider the polar curve $r={tan}^{2}⁡\theta $ for $\theta \in (-\frac{\pi }{2},\frac{\pi }{2}).$ Given that 

$$
{x}^{′}(\theta )=\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta (\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta ),\,{y}^{′}(\theta )={tan}^{2}⁡\theta \operatorname{sec}⁡\theta ({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +2),\,
$$

and ${x}^{′}(0)=0,$ which of the following statements are true?

I. ${y}^{′}(0)=0$

II. ${lim}_{\theta \to {0}^{+}}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\infty $

III. The curve has a vertical tangent at $\theta =0$
question.worked_solution:
For a given polar curve, there is a vertical tangent at $\theta ={\theta }_{0}$ if

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{y}^{′}({\theta }_{0})}{{x}^{′}({\theta }_{0})}
$$

is infinite. This means that

$$
{y}^{′}({\theta }_{0})\ne 0\,\text{and}\,{x}^{′}({\theta }_{0})=0.
$$

However, if the curve is continuous at ${\theta }_{0}$ yet the derivative takes the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0}$ at this point, we say that the curve has a vertical tangent at this point if

$$
{lim}_{\theta \to {\theta }_{0}^{-}}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\pm \infty \,\text{and}\,{lim}_{\theta \to {\theta }_{0}^{+}}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\pm \infty .
$$

In this case, we're told that ${x}^{′}(0)=0.$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. Substituting $\theta =0$ into the expression for ${y}^{′}(\theta ),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(0) & ={tan}^{2}⁡(0)\operatorname{sec}⁡(0)({cos}^{2}⁡(0)+2) \\  & =0\cdot 1\cdot ({1}^{2}+2) \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is false. Computing the limit as $\theta \to {0}^{+},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{\theta \to {0}^{+}}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & ={lim}_{\theta \to {0}^{+}}\frac{{y}^{′}(\theta )}{{x}^{′}(\theta )} \\  & ={lim}_{\theta \to {0}^{+}}(\frac{{tan}^{2}⁡\theta \operatorname{sec}⁡\theta ({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +2)}{\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta (\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta )}) \\  & ={lim}_{\theta \to {0}^{+}}(\frac{{tan}^{\cancel{2}}⁡\theta \operatorname{sec}⁡\theta ({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +2)}{\cancel{\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta }(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta )}) \\  & ={lim}_{\theta \to {0}^{+}}(\frac{\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta \operatorname{sec}⁡\theta ({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +2)}{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta }) \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{tan}⁡(0)\operatorname{sec}⁡(0)({cos}^{2}⁡(0)+2)}{\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)+\operatorname{sec}⁡(0)} \\  & =\frac{0\cdot 1\cdot ({1}^{2}+2)}{1+1} \\  & =\frac{0}{2} \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement III is false. Since the right limit of our derivative is not infinite, the curve does *not* have a vertical tangent at $\theta =0.$ In fact, it is a horizontal tangent.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14227801/assets/498b937eba18870a36ee6f09bb99cf7dde38eb95c4cc2aa6edcb46080d0fcf04.png)

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."
